strengths: The paper targets an important computer-vision problem: efficient adaptation to subject-specific variation in subtle video expressions, with potential relevance to pain and stress assessment.
Using localized facial-action descriptions as an intermediate representation is intuitive, potentially more interpretable than generic emotion prompts, and avoids LLM-generated supervision.
The frozen CLIP encoders, lightweight temporal module, AU adapter, and test-time updates provide a computationally economical design.

Experiments cover three distinct datasets and include subject-level results, several recent CLIP/TTA baselines, prompt and window-length studies, and some qualitative analysis. The authors also acknowledge the limited gains and possible over-adaptation on BAH.
weaknesses: The claimed AU foundation is technically problematic. Many of the 46 IDs do not match standard FACS definitions: for example, standard AU25 is lips part, AU27 is mouth stretch, AU43 is eyes closed, AU45 is blink, and AU46 is wink, whereas the manuscript assigns these IDs to unrelated actions. Head and gaze movements are also presented as AU30–37. Consequently, claims of anatomically grounded semantics and agreement with OpenFace are unreliable; several qualitative comparisons appear to compare incompatible labels.

CLIP-AUTT is described as subject-level personalization, but adaptation is performed independently on each video and reset afterward. It therefore never learns a persistent subject model or aggregates multiple observations of a person; it is instance-level test-time optimization. The evidence does not substantiate the central personalization claim.

The TTA comparison is confounded by initialization and representation. Competing methods use a fully fine-tuned vanilla CLIP source model, while CLIP-AUTT starts from the proposed AU-based architecture. Thus, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed adaptation. A controlled comparison applying all TTA methods to the same source representation, plus CLIP-AU with and without each test-time component on every dataset, is needed.

Important protocol details are missing: how source/target subjects were selected, whether any identities overlap with development decisions, what validation data selected the window length, prompt template, learning rate, and number of adaptation steps, and whether target labels influenced these choices. Several hyperparameters are selected using reported BioVid performance, creating a risk of test-set tuning.

The empirical study uses only one fixed set of ten target subjects per dataset, reports no repeated splits, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and includes many perfect per-subject scores. This is insufficient to establish robustness to subject variability, especially given the small and apparently uneven per-subject sample counts.

Directly optimizing 46 AU embeddings from a single unlabeled video for ten iterations can readily overfit to a confident initial prediction. Entropy minimization reinforces confirmation bias and supplies no evidence that the updated embeddings remain faithful to their textual AU meanings. No analysis of prediction flips, failure rates, calibration, adaptation stability, or sensitivity to initialization is provided.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed ingredients. There is no comprehensive factorial comparison of temporal window selection, entropy minimization, AU-embedding updates, and the unadapted model across all three datasets. The temporal-module justification relies primarily on training-statistic plots rather than matched quantitative results.

The method description is ambiguous in reproducibility-critical places: it alternately calls the temporal encoder a 1D CNN and a single linear layer, does not fully specify convolutional dimensions or the AU adapter, and is unclear whether test-time optimization updates free embeddings, prompt tokens, or adapter parameters. Computational cost is illustrated but not rigorously reported per adaptation episode.

The overall algorithmic novelty is modest: frozen CLIP similarities, a temporal CNN, low-entropy segment selection, and entropy-minimization prompt updates are mostly established components. Given the incorrect AU semantics and confounded evaluation, the manuscript does not yet demonstrate that their combination yields the claimed interpretable personalization contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: recognizing subtle, subject-dependent facial behavior while limiting the number of trainable parameters.

Using structured facial-movement descriptions as an intermediate representation is intuitively appealing, and the frozen CLIP backbone, lightweight temporal module, and text-side adaptation form a computationally efficient design.

The evaluation covers three datasets with different capture conditions and includes subject-wise results, several CLIP/TTA baselines, prompt comparisons, temporal-window experiments, and supplementary implementation details.

If the protocol is valid, the reported BioVid and StressID improvements are substantial, particularly in F1. The manuscript is generally organized and provides equations and diagrams for the main pipeline. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/0435e2f8455a43528e1f29c81268cfc1/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The novelty is limited: CLIP-AU is essentially frozen CLIP features, a lightweight temporal encoder, similarities to textual descriptors, and a supervised MLP; CLIP-AUTT combines standard entropy minimization with confidence-based window selection. The paper does not establish that this combination constitutes a sufficiently original algorithmic contribution.

The central personalization claim is not supported by the method. Section 3.2 states that adaptation is performed independently for each video and reset afterward. Thus, the method neither aggregates multiple videos from a subject nor learns a persistent subject representation; it is sample-wise test-time adaptation, not subject-level personalization. Entropy minimization on a single example merely reinforces the model's existing prediction and can amplify errors.

The purported 46 Action Units are not a valid FACS inventory. Numerous identifiers conflict with standard definitions: for example, the supplement calls AU06 'eyelids tightened' rather than cheek raiser, AU25 'eyes slitted' rather than lips part, and AU28 blink rather than lip suck. Head and gaze actions are also assigned nonstandard numbers. The abstract itself describes AU06 as cheek raiser, contradicting the supplied table. This materially undermines the paper's anatomical grounding, AU interpretation, and attribution.

The experimental protocol is too incomplete to validate the headline results. The paper does not clearly specify class definitions, video/sample counts, preprocessing and frame sampling, source train/validation splits, model-selection procedure, or whether target labels influenced subject, prompt, and hyperparameter choices. Prompt selection and window-length selection are reported directly on benchmark performance without a disclosed held-out validation protocol, creating a serious risk of target-test tuning.

The comparison is not controlled. TTA baselines appear to start from a fully fine-tuned CLIP model, whereas CLIP-AUTT builds on the AU-specific source model and classifier. Consequently, the results conflate the quality of the source representation with the proposed adaptation rule. Implementation and tuning details for adapting image-based baselines to videos are insufficient, and results lack repeated splits, random-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Essential ablations are missing. There is no clean decomposition of full-video inference, low-entropy window selection without adaptation, random/center-window selection, AU-embedding entropy adaptation without selection, and alternative adaptable parameter sets. Comparing AU prompts against 46 generic class prompts does not isolate whether semantic AU structure matters, because a supervised adapter and classifier can use the 46 similarity coordinates as arbitrary learned features.

The interpretability evidence is not convincing. Similarity to AU text after supervised adapter training is treated as AU activation without AU supervision or calibration. Directly optimizing those embeddings at test time further breaks their fixed linguistic meaning. Agreement with OpenFace is shown only through selected qualitative examples, with no quantitative AU-level evaluation, while OpenFace itself is not ground truth.

BAH exposes a major limitation obscured by the main table: supplementary Table 4 reports UAR near chance for essentially every method, with CLIP-AUTT at 50.2 versus T3AL at 51.1. Its WAR gain is therefore largely compatible with majority-class behavior, and the F1 improvement is only 0.4 points. The paper nevertheless claims robust state-of-the-art performance and omits UAR from the main comparison. It also fails to define whether F1 is macro, weighted, or micro.

There are reporting inconsistencies. The abbreviated BioVid subject table in the main paper does not transparently correspond to the complete supplementary table and includes values that cannot be reconciled from the reported subject list. The stated temporal encoder is also described inconsistently as a 1D CNN composed of a single linear layer. These issues reduce confidence in the results and reproducibility.

The manuscript makes healthcare-oriented claims about pain and stress assessment but provides no meaningful analysis of demographic bias, privacy, consent, misuse, or clinical validity. This is especially important for facial affect inference, where cultural and individual variation can make confident predictions harmful. Overall, the protocol ambiguity, invalid AU definitions, uncontrolled baselines, and mismatch between sample-wise adaptation and claimed personalization prevent a convincing scientific case.

strengths: The paper presents an appealing and practically relevant direction: structured facial-action descriptions provide a more appropriate interface to CLIP than generic emotion-class prompts for subtle video emotion recognition.

The combination of a frozen CLIP backbone, lightweight temporal module, AU adapter, and test-time embedding updates is computationally economical. The distinction between source-trained CLIP-AU and test-time CLIP-AUTT is clearly explained.

Experiments cover three meaningfully different datasets, several recent CLIP-based FER and test-time-adaptation baselines, subject-level results, temporal-window ablations, prompt controls, and efficiency analysis. The reported BioVid and StressID improvements are substantial, especially in F1.
The class-prompt replacement and AU/class-prompt fusion experiments provide useful evidence that localized facial-action descriptions contribute beyond simply supplying many text prompts.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes supplementary implementation details, subject-wise results, and explicit discussion of the difficult BAH setting.
weaknesses: The central Action Unit interpretation is technically problematic. The 46-item list does not follow canonical FACS numbering: for example, canonical AU6 is cheek raiser and AU25 is lips part, whereas the paper labels AU06 as eyelid tightening and AU25 as narrowed eyes. Head pose and gaze entries are also presented as AUs although they are normally action descriptors. Consequently, comparisons to canonical OpenFace AU outputs by nominal AU identifier are not valid, and the claimed anatomical interpretability is undermined. The method could instead be framed as using facial-action descriptions, but that would weaken a central claim.

The scores are not shown to represent actual AU activation. Training uses only emotion labels, so the adapter and classifier can repurpose the 46 similarities as arbitrary latent features. Directly optimizing unconstrained AU embeddings at test time can further move them away from their textual meanings. Selected qualitative OpenFace examples are insufficient; quantitative AU agreement, embedding-drift analysis, or evaluation on AU-annotated data is needed.

The TTA comparison does not cleanly isolate the proposed adaptation mechanism. The listed TTA baselines start from a conventionally fine-tuned CLIP model, while CLIP-AUTT starts from the stronger AU-based CLIP-AU architecture. Thus, especially on StressID, the advantage may combine a better source model with better adaptation. Existing TTA methods should be applied to the same CLIP-AU source model, alongside prompt tuning without window selection and window selection without adaptation.

Although described as subject-specific personalization, adaptation appears to be performed independently on each video and reset afterward. It neither aggregates evidence across videos belonging to the same person nor establishes that the learned update captures identity-specific behavior rather than ordinary sample-wise confidence sharpening. The terminology and claims should be narrowed or supported with genuine subject-level adaptation experiments.

The evaluation relies primarily on one set of ten selected target subjects per dataset, without repeated subject-disjoint splits, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a clearly specified validation protocol for hyperparameter and prompt selection. The BAH subject selection is particularly under-justified, creating uncertainty about robustness and possible selection bias.

The BAH results are much less convincing than the headline WAR suggests: UAR remains near chance (50.2), F1 improves only from 40.7 to 41.1 over T3AL, and several individual subjects become worse. Reporting only WAR and F1 in the main comparison obscures this near-majority-class behavior.

Minimum class-posterior entropy is treated as evidence of the most expressive temporal segment, but confidence need not correspond to expression intensity and may favor easy neutral or spurious segments. The method assumes one stable video-level expression and can reinforce an initially incorrect prediction. Oracle/annotation-based peak comparisons and failure analysis are needed.

Several reproducibility details remain unclear, including class definitions and sample counts per split, clip construction and frame sampling, face preprocessing, the exact parameters optimized at test time, learning rates for adaptation, and validation data used to choose window length and prompts. The supplementary gradient explanation also resembles an argmax pseudo-label gradient rather than an exact derivation of the stated entropy objective. Overall, the idea and empirical signals are promising, but the semantic-validity and evaluation-control issues currently favor a borderline rejection under the default Algorithms/General category.

strengths: The manuscript presents a relevant idea: using localized facial-action descriptions as CLIP prompts and adapting them at test time for subtle video emotion recognition. The overall pipeline is intuitive and computationally lightweight. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/b7a3162438024cbabc1b0021cd4668d6/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported results are promising across BioVid, StressID, and BAH. CLIP-AU generally improves over the presented supervised CLIP baselines, while CLIP-AUTT obtains the best average WAR and F1 among the evaluated TTA approaches, with particularly large gains on StressID.

The paper includes useful component studies covering window length, prompt type, AU-adapter use, temporal architecture, sampling rate, and the separate effects of window selection and prompt tuning. Per-subject tables expose substantial heterogeneity that aggregate results alone would conceal.

The method freezes the large CLIP encoders and adapts only lightweight components, which is attractive for test-time deployment. The paper also acknowledges weaker performance and possible over-adaptation on the challenging BAH dataset.
weaknesses: The central AU formulation contains serious factual inconsistencies. The supplied list does not follow standard FACS numbering: for example, standard AU4 is brow lowerer, AU5 is upper-lid raiser, AU6 is cheek raiser, AU23 is lip tightener, and AU25 is lips part, whereas Table S1 assigns different actions to these identifiers and invents a sequential 1–46 taxonomy containing head and gaze movements. The main text itself calls AU06 both “cheek raiser” and “eyelids tightened.” This undermines the anatomical grounding and interpretability claimed as the paper's main contribution.

There is no convincing evidence that the similarity coordinates actually represent AU activations. They receive no AU supervision, are optimized only through emotion labels, and can consequently become arbitrary discriminative latent features. The OpenFace evidence consists of selected qualitative examples without a quantitative AU agreement metric; moreover, OpenFace uses standard FACS identifiers, making comparison against the paper's incompatible AU numbering especially questionable.

The claimed subject-level personalization is not clearly realized by the algorithm. The paper states that adaptation is performed independently for each video and reset afterward, and the supplement says each video receives ten iterations. This is per-video transductive adaptation rather than learning a subject-specific model across that subject's videos. No experiment compares video-wise adaptation with genuine subject-stream adaptation or shows that the updates encode stable traits of an individual.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified and potentially fragile. Class definitions, video/sample counts, class distributions, source/validation splitting, model-selection procedure, and whether all hyperparameters were chosen without target-test feedback are missing. Results rely mainly on one fixed set of ten target subjects per dataset rather than cross-subject folds or repeated subject sampling. Seed variability is reported only for StressID, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals support statements such as “significantly informative.”

Baseline comparability is unclear. CLIP-AUTT starts from the custom supervised CLIP-AU representation and classifier, whereas several baselines operate through class prompts or other adaptation interfaces; the paper does not establish that every TTA method receives an equivalent source model, temporal input, augmentation budget, number of optimization steps, or hyperparameter tuning budget. The apparent collapse of the generic-prompt TTA baseline on StressID further calls for diagnostic analysis.

Entropy selects the model's already most confident window and then sharpens its prediction on that same window. This can reinforce erroneous predictions through confirmation bias, but the paper does not measure pseudo-label correctness before adaptation, performance conditioned on selection errors, calibration, or failure rates. The wording also conflates minimum predictive entropy with the “most expressive” segment, which does not follow without external temporal annotations.

Reproducibility is limited: the abstract contains an empty “Our code:” field, important architectural dimensions and adaptation hyperparameters are absent, and the exact preprocessing, face detection/alignment, augmentation, and baseline implementation details are not given. For a method motivated by pain and stress assessment, the paper also lacks analysis of demographic bias, privacy, clinical reliability, and consequences of erroneous predictions.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/0c16fdd54489429d99b1837a6b724447/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a relevant problem: efficient adaptation of video emotion recognition to individual variation, with potential value for pain and stress analysis.
The proposed pipeline is computationally lightweight: CLIP is frozen, temporal information is modeled with a compact 1D-CNN/GLU module, and adaptation updates only text-side representations.

Experiments cover three subtle-expression datasets plus FERV39K, compare against several CLIP and test-time-adaptation methods, and include component, window-length, prompt-design, sampling-rate, and limited multi-seed analyses.
The reported gains are sizeable, especially on StressID, and the subject-wise tables expose substantial variability that aggregate metrics alone would hide.
weaknesses: The core AU formulation is technically unsound. The purported FACS identifiers are systematically inconsistent with standard FACS nomenclature: for example, brow lowering is AU4 rather than the paper's AU03, upper-lid raising is AU5 rather than AU04, cheek raising is AU6 rather than AU05, lid tightening is AU7 rather than AU06, nose wrinkling is AU9 rather than AU07, and smiling/lip-corner pulling is AU12 rather than AU10. Head and eye movements are likewise assigned nonstandard sequential identifiers. This invalidates the claim that the 46 prompts are anatomically grounded FACS AUs and makes the OpenFace comparison difficult or impossible to interpret correctly.

The method never learns or verifies AU detection. Training uses only emotion-label cross-entropy; there is no AU annotation, AU alignment objective, or quantitative AU evaluation. A trainable text adapter followed by an emotion classifier can repurpose the 46 similarities as arbitrary class-discriminative features. Consequently, calling them AU activation strengths, interpreting their rankings anatomically, and claiming improved AU-video alignment are unsupported. The few hand-selected OpenFace visualizations do not resolve this issue, particularly given the incompatible AU definitions.

The claimed subject-level personalization is actually per-video transductive adaptation. The manuscript states that parameters are adapted independently for each video and reset afterward, so information is not accumulated across videos belonging to a subject. The method therefore cannot substantiate claims that it learns an individual's expressive style or distinctive subject-level AU pattern; it is more accurately sample-level entropy minimization.

The adaptation objective simply minimizes the entropy of the model's own prediction on a window selected for already having minimum entropy. This can reinforce an incorrect initial prediction through confirmation bias. No mechanism establishes that low entropy corresponds to peak expression rather than an easy neutral segment, and no oracle temporal annotations or quantitative peak-window evaluation support that interpretation.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently controlled for the magnitude of the claims. Only 10 selected target subjects per dataset form the main evaluation, with no repeated subject splits or confidence intervals across subjects. Selection criteria are vague, particularly for BAH, and hyperparameter selection on target subjects is not explained. Most results are single runs; the sole three-seed StressID analysis reports averages that differ from the headline table without reconciliation.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are unclear. The compared TTA methods were designed for different image/video settings and are adapted here without enough implementation detail, while the proposed method and baselines do not evidently share an identical source model, temporal representation, augmentation budget, or number of updates. Comparisons against directly relevant video TTA and FER personalization/SFDA methods are also missing despite their discussion in related work.

Critical protocol details are absent or ambiguous: dataset class definitions and sample counts, train/validation/test construction, face preprocessing, video/frame sampling, sliding-window stride, final post-adaptation inference procedure, exact tuned parameterization, augmentation, and how learning rates and window length were selected. The abstract's code link is blank, further limiting reproducibility.

Some headline evidence is weak or internally troubling. On BAH, nearly every method has approximately 50% UAR while WAR reaches 70%, indicating majority-class behavior; CLIP-AUTT's F1 gain over T3AL is only 0.4 points. Perfect per-subject scores and very large StressID gains receive no uncertainty or diagnostic analysis. FERV39K is reported only against one baseline per group and lacks protocol details.

Novelty is limited under the default Algorithms/General contribution type: the system mainly combines AU-like textual phrases, a conventional temporal encoder, minimum-entropy window selection, and standard test-time entropy minimization. The paper does not provide sufficient technical or empirical support to elevate this combination beyond an incremental construction.

For a system motivated by healthcare-related pain and stress assessment, the manuscript does not adequately discuss demographic bias, privacy, cultural dependence, clinical misuse, or the danger of confident but incorrect personalization. These concerns are particularly material because entropy minimization explicitly increases confidence without validating correctness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: efficient personalization of video-based recognition for subtle pain, stress, and ambivalence expressions. The proposed combination of structured facial-action prompts, temporal modeling, and test-time adaptation is intuitive and potentially useful.

The empirical results are promising. CLIP-AU improves substantially over the reported CLIP-based FER baselines on BioVid and BAH, while CLIP-AUTT achieves the best reported WAR and F1 on all three principal datasets; the gains on BioVid and especially StressID are sizable.

The evaluation includes subject-wise results, component ablations, temporal-window studies, prompt comparisons, sampling-rate analysis, an additional FERV39K experiment, and an efficiency discussion. These analyses provide more evidence than a single aggregate benchmark table.
The method is lightweight: the CLIP encoders remain frozen, while temporal and prompt-side components are adapted. This is attractive for privacy-sensitive or resource-constrained applications.

The manuscript is generally well organized, visually clear, and candid about difficulty on BAH, where facial cues are ambiguous and environmental variation is greater. Assessment is based on the complete manuscript and supplement: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/5d282253332e45fdb8e1cf8f4efe9eef/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The claimed FACS grounding appears technically incorrect. The table calls 46 sequentially numbered cues Action Units, but numerous identifiers do not match canonical FACS definitions—for example, AU25 is described as narrow eye opening rather than lips part, AU30 as head turn left rather than jaw sideways, and AU46 as tongue show rather than wink. This is not a cosmetic nomenclature issue: anatomical grounding and interpretability are central claims of the paper.

The qualitative validation with OpenFace is consequently questionable. The paper presents cues such as AU37/eye-look-down as outputs of an external AU detector, although OpenFace does not ordinarily estimate the full custom 46-cue inventory shown here. The exact mapping from OpenFace outputs to these prompts and a quantitative AU-agreement evaluation are missing.

CLIP-AUTT directly optimizes AU embeddings by minimizing entropy on the same test video being classified. Without an anchor, regularizer, or AU supervision, those embeddings need not retain their original AU meanings. Entropy minimization can simply reinforce the initial class prediction, so improved confidence does not establish personalized AU alignment; this also weakens interpretation of post-adaptation top-AU visualizations.

The method is described as subject-level personalization, yet the paper states that adaptation is performed independently for each video and reset afterward. This is more accurately sample/video-level test-time adaptation and does not learn persistent traits from multiple observations of a subject. The central personalization claim should therefore be narrowed or supported with a genuine subject-stream protocol.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified for firm conclusions: only ten target subjects are used per dataset; selection, validation, class construction, video counts, window stride, and hyperparameter-selection procedures are unclear. There are no confidence intervals over target-subject splits, and three-seed statistics are reported only for StressID. It is therefore difficult to exclude split-selection or test-set tuning effects.

Results on BAH are weak in balanced terms: supplementary UAR remains approximately chance level (50.2%) and is below T3AL (51.1%), while the F1 improvement is only 0.4 points. Reporting mainly WAR and F1 in the main paper overstates the robustness of the claimed advance on this highly imbalanced dataset.

Baseline fairness needs stronger support. Most comparisons are generic image-level TTA methods adapted to video, while relevant personalized FER/SFDA approaches discussed in related work are not evaluated. Details establishing identical video sampling, augmentation, update budgets, model initialization, and tuning access across baselines are limited.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate: the code link is blank, and some implementation descriptions are inconsistent or incomplete—for example, the temporal encoder is called a 1D CNN but is also described as a single linear layer. Overall, the idea and results are encouraging, but the AU-ontology error and unvalidated semantic interpretation affect the core scientific case, yielding a slight preference for rejection pending correction and stronger evaluation.
